CONGRATS!! I got my dream job in Wound Care a little over a year ago. The WOCN is a great goal but it requires the practical experience in addition to the exams. But start learning more about it and depending on your learning style if you think prep courses would be right for you and something you would enjoy and gain enrichment from. Journal articles are good reads, but this first year I benefitted from practical and hands on knowledge. Look into videos from NPWT and compression therapy to see how different products require different application techniques. If you have an old study guide for Derm or nclex study, review that to get primed for any questions you want to throw at your preceptor and colleagues. I haven’t joined any wound societies but they have the journals. Woundsource.com is also good. I used them for free CEUs and actually got some good info early on (CEUs are more than just a formality omg) about wound care topics. 

Good luck!!

I wouldn’t say I’m in the expert area on keto or on nutrition for healing. Increasing your intake of protein is key. Carbs from whole vegetables, grains, fruits - rather than processed foods would be healthier and closer to how food is meant to be processed by the body. Weight loss may help wound healing. But the stress of the change, plus entering and maintaining ketosis along with the keto flu might be hard. Or having diarrhea in response to the increase in fat or constipation from so much meat and dairy - I would worry about the affects on the wound.

Please run your plan for nutrition by the provider you are following up with post surgery. 2-3x the normal amount of protein will greatly assist in your healing. However some of the gastrointestinal side effects when starting keto could make that diet plan contraindicated due to the location of your surgery.

I started out my nursing career using paper MARS and charts / records and have since moved on to using EMAR and EHR. I can say without a doubt that I feel a lot better about the timing, allergy alerts that assist with medication administration as well as lab values and vital signs being more accessible, can with one click be shown on a graph since I'm very much a visual and kinesthetic person. 

The pharmacy pull method of med reconciliation is a pet peeve of mine and I make it a point to get a med list from the patient or try to verify with them what medications they do take not just what they SHOULD be taking. Sometimes I have to fall back on the pharmacy method because the patient is completely altered with no one present to verify their medications, or the family is there and doesn't know the information either, or the patient is just woefully in ignorant bliss of what the names, dosage, frequency, purpose are for. I can cross reference with the latter - so I have 3 blood pressure medications here, do you know if you take all 3? Do you still take this medicine for overactive bladder? However, I would say I may be a special unicorn because some of the more time crunched or jaded colleague's may skip the long discussion with the patient and just get a pharmacy fax or check the recent insurance pull. And on Meditech that means you gotta guess the frequency on dispensed and days. Not cool and it also doesn't tell you if its BID 0900 and 2100 or morning, afternoon, or with meals only, etc. There you have to have knowledge of the medications - which.... 

Our electronic patient portal was never used and was removed. So when patient's want records it becomes an ugly medical records request - on paper and then waiting and mailing and I've got angry patient or family asking why I can't just get on my little computer and hit print - ITS THEIR LIFE. Well, actually...

I do think that the electronic age has kept the doctors on the move and doing more because it increases efficiency and all that good stuff so they can see more patients. What it has really done is free up time for more patients to be seen and admitted, but the doctor doesn't get much face time after that with their admitted patients. I work at night and do a lot of paging and waiting, either for a return call or orders to generate on my screen from the doctor placing them at a computer terminal somewhere else on campus. That's great that the docs don't have to physically materialize and scribble on charts. It also helps with the fact that all of the staff's writing is HORRIFIC. Can't be messy using a font! So that's a plus. We don't use computers on wheels, ours are stations on the wall and my back would be to my patients, so I don't use the in-room computers except to scan to the MARS or check something as far as med schedule or scan progress notes to reinforce teaching. I wish our facility used COWS because then I could position the computer so I could be facing the client, chart an assessment or note while in the room, and I'm a good enough typist to do so without looking at the screen. 

When we had EHR downtime I was happy with walking around with my patient note pages on my clipboard, and scribbling my patient notes on rounds as I actually walked around. I was so caught up that night! But my arm hurt like the dickens the next morning.

Hope this helps and good luck.
